extracted.intended_audience: tourists / travellers planning to visit Edinburgh (general public)
extracted.subtask_description: A city-level travel guide describing districts, transport, sights, accommodation, safety and practical advice for visiting Edinburgh. It is meant to help travellers plan logistics, timing, and on-the-ground behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to go / busy periods and booking advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Edinburgh is a year-round destination. It gets very busy around New Year (Hogmanay), the Six Nations rugby internationals in Feb/March, and particularly during the Fringe Festivals in August - book accommodation well in advance for these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book accommodation well in advance for festival time (the page later emphasises booking at least six months ahead for August festival season). Consider quieter months if you want to avoid crowds and premium pricing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate / weather expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Old and New Towns are on exposed ridges so they're often breezy, and you can expect rain and a wrecked umbrella any day. The city is most comfortable from May to September.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summer has long daylight (sunrise ~4:30AM, sunset ~10PM); winters are 'snell' with wind-chill and short daylight (sun up ~8:30AM–4PM). Pack for wind and rain year-round.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodation registration legal requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All short-term accommodation in Scotland must be registered, otherwise it's illegal and probably a flea-pit or fire-trap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal requirement (introduced 2022) is especially pertinent in Edinburgh where demand encourages exploitative providers. Be sceptical of unregistered providers; registration deadlines and enforcement may evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Walking as primary mode within centre
rubrics_metrics.description: Walking should always be your first choice within central Edinburgh. The centre is compact - most sights and attractions are on or near the Royal Mile in Old Town or Princes St in New Town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in hills, railway barriers and deep glens which can make some routes longer or steeper; comfortable shoes recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public transport ticketing for trams
rubrics_metrics.description: You must buy a tram ticket before boarding the tram. Machines at tram stops accept cards and coins (5p to £2 coins, no change given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tram fares: single journey excluding airport cheaper, airport single is more expensive. Day tickets can be valid across trams and daytime buses; check current fares and buy within 30 minutes of starting travel if using tram machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public transport ticketing for buses
rubrics_metrics.description: Buy tickets on boarding the bus either with exact fare in coins (no change is given) or by contactless debit/credit card. A single ticket is a flat fare regardless of distance and with no transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you make three or more journeys on the same day with the same contactless card, fare is automatically capped at the day-ticket price. Night fares and family or student fares differ; have correct payment method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Airlink 100 airport bus specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Airlink 100 runs to city centre from the airport and operates 24 hours every 10–20 minutes, taking 20–30 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay the driver in cash (exact fare only) or by contactless card. Buses offer free Wi‑Fi, charging sockets and CCTV and have next‑stop info screens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tram vs Airlink / airport transport trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Trams run from the airport but are generally more expensive and slower than the Airlink bus; airport tram single fares are higher and you must buy before boarding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multi-day tickets valid on tram and daytime buses for savings; compare tram/ bus times and prices before travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Left luggage advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Left luggage at Waverley station costs £15 per item per 24 hours (much more expensive than at the main bus station).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bus station lockers for cheaper left luggage; check current prices and opening hours before travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train travel booking and sleeper guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Daytime trains from London to Edinburgh run hourly; Caledonian Lowland Sleeper and other sleeper services have compartments sold like hotel rooms and are bookable up to 12 months ahead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sleeper compartments cost extra and pricing is dynamic; you may need to print e-tickets; no Saturday overnight service on some sleepers. Check whether you can stay aboard until 8AM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Park and ride / driving advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Edinburgh is not a car-friendly city, with many central streets closed-off or dead-ended to private vehicles. Use park and ride facilities on the city's edge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are seven park and ride sites serving different approaches. Central parking is scarce and expensive; expect parking wardens to be zealous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low Emission Zone (LEZ) compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: From 1 June 2024, the Old and New Town will be a Low Emission Zone, with camera-enforced penalties for entering in a non-compliant vehicle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cars built after 2015 are generally compliant, but travellers should check online for vehicle compliance before driving into the zone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parking fines and towing penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Parking fines are £100 and vehicles parked in an obstructive manner are liable to be towed away with a £150 release fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid illegal or obstructive parking. Use the Council interactive map for Pay and Display bays and charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed limits in city centre
rubrics_metrics.description: Edinburgh has a 20 mph (32 km/h) speed limit on many roads in the city centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drivers should comply with local speed signage; enforcement is typical of UK urban areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety: pickpockets and intoxicated people
rubrics_metrics.description: In general Edinburgh is a safe destination. Take care of valuables, especially in crowded places where pickpockets operate. Swerve clear of drunks, especially after football matches and at pub closing times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rundown areas mentioned (examples given); in an emergency dial 999 (or 112); non-emergency police number 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health / medical emergency contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: In emergency, dial 999 (preferably from a landline). For non-emergency medical problems ring NHS 24 on 111 (textphone 18001 111).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh hosts the main A&E and other clinics have specific opening hours; check details before travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmacy availability
rubrics_metrics.description: During normal shopping hours pharmacies are widespread, but there are no 24 h pharmacies in the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For late or Sunday openings call NHS Inform or check online to find which pharmacies are open outside normal hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Booking and entry for major attractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Edinburgh Castle often sells out in summer; best book online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some festival events have preview or discounted tickets; planning ahead can yield cheaper options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festival season planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether you wish to go at festival time (early August–mid-September); hotel rooms are much more expensive and you will need to book at least six months in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Festival programming includes International Festival, Military Tattoo, Fringe; preview performances and special ticket offers can reduce cost if you plan carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tram and bus ticket products and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Day tickets (for tram and daytime buses) are available; PLUSBUS rail add-on allows travel on tram but not to the airport. A single bus ticket is a flat fare with no transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check exclusions (sightseeing buses, night buses, airport) and whether rail add-ons cover your route before purchasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using contactless cards and fare capping
rubrics_metrics.description: Paying by contactless debit/credit card is accepted on many buses and avoids carrying exact change; if you make three or more journeys on the same day on the same card, your fare is automatically capped at the day-ticket price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contactless may not always be accepted (e.g., some tram machines) so carry a backup payment method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxi etiquette and booking
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Black Cabs (up to 5 passengers) can be hailed on the street and display an orange light when available; minicabs must be pre-booked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of main firms provided; taxi ranks near stations and main streets make finding a cab straightforward in central areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cycle hire and routes
rubrics_metrics.description: VOI app-based scheme includes e-bikes and e-scooters; local hire companies and National Cycle Network routes provide wide access for cyclists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many off-street paths, route 1 to Melrose for weekend trips; check hire prices and operating times for vendors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional onward travel suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Edinburgh is well-connected for day trips across Scotland and to nearby towns; suggestions include South Queensferry, Linlithgow, Stirling, Glasgow, North Berwick, Dunbar etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose destinations based on available transport (train/bus) and time available; many are reasonable day trips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local money handling and banknote quirks
rubrics_metrics.description: Scottish, English and Northern Irish banknotes are all acceptable. Bank of Scotland and RBS issue their own notes which their ATMs dispense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retailers are obliged to accept Scottish notes, but exchange desks may be sniffy or give poor rates; be mindful when returning home with Scottish notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visitor information and official sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Forever Edinburgh is the city's official guide listing attractions and forthcoming events; City of Edinburgh Council describes public services; iCentre is the national tourist office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use official sources for up-to-date event listings, transport changes and public service information.
